flagged.evidence: Step 1.1 applies [L2] to conclude |ν_a|(X)=∫|dν_a/dμ|dμ before either side of the claimed equivalence has established that ν_a is finite. But [L2] explicitly says: “For an absolutely continuous finite signed or finite complex measure, the total variation has density …”. The Statement permits a nonfinite signed ν_a; for example ν_a=λ relative to λ on R satisfies the decomposition hypotheses but is not finite. Thus [L2] does not license step 1.1 in the case needed to prove the reverse implication.

The Remark says “the functional g↦∫g dν is bounded on L²(μ) when ν≪μ and finite”. Take μ=λ on (0,1) and dν=x^{-1/2}dλ. Then ν is finite and ν≪μ, but h=x^{-1/2} is not in L²(μ). With g_n=h·1_{[1/n,1]}/||h·1_{[1/n,1]}||₂, one has ||g_n||₂=1 while ∫g_n dν=||h·1_{[1/n,1]}||₂→∞. Hence this functional is not bounded on L²(μ).

The Statement assumes only that λ and μ are sigma-finite and that ν is “a signed measure … with ν≪μ≪λ”. Its cited definition says a signed-measure derivative is defined only “if ν is a signed measure satisfying the hypothesis of [thm-radon-nikodym-density-exists-and-is-unique-up-to-almost-everywhere-equality]”, whose Statement requires a common exhaustion X_n with μ(X_n),|ν|(X_n)<∞. That condition is absent here, so dν/dμ and dν/dλ need not be defined in the repository’s sense. Concretely, on [0,1] let λ=μ be Lebesgue measure and let ν(E)=0 for λ(E)=0 and ν(E)=+∞ otherwise. This is a positive (hence signed) measure with ν≪μ but has no such finite exhaustion and no real-valued representing density; nevertheless it satisfies the written hypotheses.

The Statement permits an arbitrary positive measure μ. Yet [L1] invokes dν/dμ and cites the total-variation density theorem. The cited definition begins “Let μ be a sigma-finite positive measure”, and the cited total-variation theorem likewise begins “Let μ be a sigma-finite positive measure.” No sigma-finiteness of μ appears in this Statement. Thus the density formula and its integrability used in step 1.1 are not licensed; finite ν does not repair this, as finite Lebesgue measure on [0,1] has no density with respect to counting measure there.

After obtaining |ν|(E)=∫_E|h|d|ν|, the proof takes E=X and states “The integrand is nonnegative” for 1−|h|. No preceding step establishes |h|≤1 almost everywhere, so that assertion does not follow from the displayed equality at E=X. The needed conclusion can be recovered quickly by applying the equality for every measurable E (for example to {|h|>1} and {|h|<1}), but that argument is absent.
